body.text: The Victorian election is one day away, with the Coalition hoping to unseat a Labor government that has enjoyed three consecutive terms in power.

Yesterday, Liberal leader Jess Wilson revealed the Coalition would partly privatise the sewerage network, cull and delay various level crossing removals, and cancel the current government's plans to expand free kinder.

Coalition looks likely to win but still lots up in the air, says ABC's Chief Election Analyst
ABC Chief Election Analyst Casey Briggs says there is plenty still up in the air despite strong polling from the Coalition ahead of the state election tomorrow.
The Coalition needs to gain 16 seats to get to the magic number of 45 seats and form a majority government.
Anything short of that will need the support of minor parties.
Briggs has told 774 ABC Melbourne, the way votes fall across individual parts of Melbourne and Victoria could have a big impact on the way parliament looks in a few days time.

"The real uncertainty at this point seems to be, is it a not great defeat, a bad defeat or a truly diabolical result for Labor? And is the Coalition going to get to majority, a comfortable majority? Or will they need to work with One Nation? I think the chances of that have receded in the last month or so," he says.

"There is a really complicated patchwork of seats at the moment. And the way those votes fall across individual parts of Melbourne and Victoria are going to have a really big impact on what the next parliament looks like."
Key Event
Former ombudsman Deborah Glass calls for earlier costings
Transparency International Australia says all political parties should be required to publish their costings well ahead of election day.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has defended her decision to release her figures and detailed policies just two days before the state election, including plans to partly privatise the state's sewerage network, delay level crossing removals and scrap the expansion of free kindergarten.
"Releasing election costings two days before polling day means many voters miss the chance to weigh up what the parties' promises will cost before they cast their ballot," chair Deborah Glass says.

"Mandating the release of these costings by a fixed date would provide voters with the information needed to make informed decisions, enhance trust in the political process, and reduce the risk of misinformation during campaigns."
While the major parties have released their costings, One Nation has also not released costings for its policies.
The party says it needs to see the state's books before attaching dollar figures to its promises.
The Jess Express pulls into the premier's electorate
Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has taken her Liberal bus to the premier's seat of Niddrie on the final day of the campaign.
Ben Carroll is at risk of losing the seat, which includes suburbs such as Airport West.
Wilson brought the travelling press pack to a pre-poll booth in the electorate.
She brought her son Patrick onto the "Jess Express" so he could "say goodbye to mummy bus".
Seats in focus: Sunbury
Sunbury was created ahead of the 2014 election, when the electoral boundaries in Melbourne's west were reconfigured to account for large population growth.
Its territory was previously covered by the regional seat of Macedon and the outer-suburban seat of Yuroke, both traditional Labor seats.
Current member Josh Bull has been the seat's only representative.
Bull's first victory in 2014 was somewhat tight but his margin blew out to more than 14 per cent on a two-party basis in Labor's landslide 2018 election.
In 2022, however, it came back down and his primary vote dropped to 43 per cent.
The seat is widely considered to be vulnerable going into this election and its demographics indicate it may be particularly suited to One Nation.
Education union slams Coalition's kinder cuts
The Australian Education Union (AEU) has called on the Coalition to commit to a full free kindergarten rollout.

It comes after Liberal leader Jess Wilson announced she'd cut back Labor's plan for 15 more hours of free kinder — something the AEU says will affect early childhood education, potentially lead to educator cuts and hit parents' hip pockets.

"Jess Wilson and the Liberal-National Coalition's planned cuts will hit children at a critical stage of their learning and development. They are unacceptable and must not happen," AEU president Justin Mullaly says.
"This is disastrous policy from the Victorian Coalition, and the way it was communicated is a slap in the face for families, teachers, and educators, some of whom may be facing the sack."
The planned cuts to four-year-old kindergarten, which is quite a significant announcement, were only made public yesterday after roughly 2 million Victorians had already voted.
Mullaly says early learning is vital to give children the best start in life

"Limiting preschool to just 15 hours a week flies in the face of all the evidence about the value of early education to make sure children are set up to thrive when they start school, especially for our most vulnerable children," he says. "The loss of free kindergarten and decreased hours for four-year-old kindergarten provision denies families equity of access and affordability."

He says parents will end up paying the price through higher fees in a cost-of-living crisis.
Key Event
Coalition to make cuts to free kinder expansion
A plan to build new kindergartens in so-called "childcare deserts" would be scrapped by a Coalition government as part of its plan to cut spending.
The kinder deserts are areas identified in Victoria with a lack of kinder spots for families, so the state was going to build and operate some centres.
But hidden in Liberal leader Jess Wilson's election costing is a half-a-billion-dollar cut to capital works for early childhood centres.
The Coalition is also saving another $400 million by not expanding access to free kinder to 30 hours a week. Families currently receive 15 hours a week of state-funded kinder.
The Coalition is set to undertake an Early Learning Structural Review to help identify gaps in the sector and assess infrastructure capacity.
It says it will ensure future early childhood facilities are built where there is genuine local need.
The Coalition is not convinced Labor's plans do that.

The ABC understands Labor's establishment of an early learning centre at Sunbury Secondary College (not Sunbury Primary School or by using existing places at existing non-government early learning centres) was a key reason for the opposition to include this area in its review.
Key Event
Key policies missing when Wilson outlined Coalition's plan
Victoria's opposition unveiled major policies on kindergarten and the partial privatisation of public assets yesterday, just two days out from the election.
At the time, roughly 2 million Victorians had already cast their ballots.
